title: Lech Lecha: the road ran everywhere
hook: a man leaves home, and his family's road runs to Kochi, Mumbai and the mountains of Ethiopia

segments.voice: Yesterday, ten generations of waiting, and Terah stopping in Haran. Your line was ten generations. Now his son picks up the road. A new portion: Lech Lecha. Day one hundred seventy-one.

Three scenes. In Kochi, on the southwest coast of India, a synagogue more than four hundred years old has a floor of hand-painted blue and white tiles from China. Up the coast near Mumbai, a community of oil pressers was known for generations by a nickname: the Saturday oil-men, because they would not work on Saturday. And in the mountains of Ethiopia, once a year, people climb to a high place in white clothes to pray and renew a promise. Every one of these is a Jewish scene. Today's portion opens with the man whose leaving started it all.
screen: `TILES FROM CHINA, IN KOCHI.` → `THE SATURDAY OIL-MEN.` → `A MOUNTAIN IN ETHIOPIA.`

segments.voice: You met the call itself on day thirty-seven: "Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house." And then, simply: "So Abram went." The family story of the Jewish people begins with someone leaving home, and the road didn't stop with him. Over the centuries Jewish families settled almost everywhere, and each community kept the same Torah while cooking, singing and dressing like its neighbors. You may know the Ashkenazi branch best: central and eastern Europe, Yiddish, the words you met on day three. Sephardi Jews trace their families to Spain and Portugal, and after 1492 carried their Judeo-Spanish language across the Mediterranean. Mizrahi Jews lived for many centuries in Iraq, Iran, Yemen, Syria and North Africa; the Jews of Iraq trace their community back to the exile in Babylon. In India there are several communities. The Jews of Cochin, with that tiled synagogue. The Bene Israel near Mumbai, whose tradition says their ancestors were shipwrecked on the coast long ago, and who kept Shabbat when they had almost nothing else. And Baghdadi Jews, traders who came later to Mumbai and Kolkata. In Ethiopia, the Beta Israel kept the Torah in the old Ge'ez language, led by their own priests, and fifty days after Yom Kippur they climb a mountain for the festival of Sigd. Today many of these families live in Israel, North America and around the world. So if Jewish brings to mind bagels and Yiddish, that's real, and it's one branch of a very big tree.
screen: `SO ABRAM WENT.` · `ASHKENAZI, SEPHARDI, MIZRAHI.` · `COCHIN, BENE ISRAEL, BAGHDADI.` · `BETA ISRAEL AND SIGD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: travel the map. Settle, and breathe. Picture a map of the world. Start where Abram started, somewhere between two rivers. Now let little lights come on: Kochi, Mumbai, Baghdad, Sana'a, Fez, Seville, Vilna, a mountain in Ethiopia, a street near you. Every light is a kitchen, a synagogue, a family keeping Shabbat in its own way. Stay with whichever one surprises you. If you pray, you can pray for every one of those tables. The bell holds the time.
Lech Lecha. Go forth: the call to Abram, and the start of a road that led Jewish families to nearly every corner of the world.
Your line: the road ran everywhere. One man left home, and his family's story now speaks many languages. Day one hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Jewish communities around the world, Ashkenazi, Sephardi, Mizrahi, Indian, Ethiopian and many more, read the same weekly Torah portion, each with its own melodies, foods, customs and languages.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jewish means one culture, from one place.
what it means: since Abram left home, Jewish families have lived almost everywhere, keeping one Torah in many languages.
what a scholar hears: the Bene Israel were known in Marathi as Shanivar Teli, Saturday oil-pressers; the Beta Israel's Torah, the Orit, is in Ge'ez, and Sigd falls on the 29th of Cheshvan.

notes: Rewritten 2026-10-06 from the five-year map; confirm with the Keeper.

Replaces 'Lech Lecha: go to yourself', which repeated day 37 (Go forth): the same verse, the same Rashi, the same Hasidic 'go to yourself', the same note on the order country/birthplace/father's house. That content still lives in day 37.

Why: 'not all Jews are of European descent' (India, Ethiopia, Mizrahi, Sephardi) was the single top-voted reply in the Reddit research; the curriculum taught it in year 3 (days 983–988). Those deeper days stay as they are.

Facts to confirm: Paradesi Synagogue (1568) floor of hand-painted Chinese tiles (18th century); Bene Israel nickname Shanivar Teli and shipwreck tradition; Baghdadi Jews in Mumbai and Kolkata (19th century); Beta Israel Orit in Ge'ez, kessim, Sigd on 29 Cheshvan, fifty days after Yom Kippur; Iraqi Jews tracing their community to the Babylonian exile.
Sigd also includes a fast in the morning; deliberately not mentioned here. If a later edit adds it, include the health line (life and health come first).
SENSITIVE: Israel is mentioned only as one place where these families now live, alongside North America and elsewhere; no politics. Keep it that way.
Word kept as 'Lech Lecha', following the camp 4 convention (each portion day's word is the portion's name).
